positioning.text: SenDISA, an AI engine that fuses video, ANPR, GPS, LiDAR and acoustic data into court-grade evidence and automated workflows for government. Sold as a detection and intelligence layer that runs on cameras a city already owns.

target_customers.text: Large cities and transport agencies buying curbside enforcement at scale: Calgary, Montreal, Toronto, Brisbane, Singapore, Philadelphia, Pittsburgh, Mississauga.
27 Smart City customers in North America at FY26 close, reached largely through channel partners rather than direct sales.
Fuel retail chains in Australia (Ampol and other brands) for forecourt drive-off detection, a non-government revenue line.

key_capabilities.text: Runs on the city's existing camera estate and VMS rather than a proprietary meter or sensor fleet, which removes the day-one hardware bill.
One engine spans parking and curb, road defects (40-plus types with severity ratings), asset and signage cataloguing, and worksite safety from the same patrol pass.
Human-in-the-loop by design: the AI detects and evidences, a trained officer reviews every event and makes every enforcement decision.
Australian deployments run 100% from Sydney and Melbourne Azure regions, geo-redundant and IRAP Protected, with no data leaving Australian borders.
ALPR accuracy stated at over 98% in all weather conditions, with evidence packages compiled at 99% accuracy to reduce litigation.
Open REST APIs and webhooks into existing ERP, GIS, asset, ticketing, payment and permit systems, with 200-plus technology partners.

battlecards.overview: A four-year-old private-equity rollup that owns the ANZ infringement back office: meters, sensors, payments, permits and PinForce on one contract, now moving to its second PE owner in four years.
battlecards.tldr: We win when the city wants AI detection across cameras it already owns, and wants more than parking out of the patrol. We lose when procurement wants one contract for meters, payments, permits and infringement processing - and in Victoria, where PinForce is already the statutory system of record.
battlecards.quick_dismiss: Orikan is strongest as the infringement back office and the hardware estate. Worth noting how the ACT structured its own A$278M programme this month: Orikan won the parking and infringement management system, while the AI camera detection contract went to a detection specialist, Acusensus. That detection scope is road safety - speed, red light, mobile phone, seatbelt - not parking. But it shows a major government buyer separating AI detection from parking and infringement processing, and not buying the detection from Orikan.

where_we_win.headline: Even Orikan's biggest win did not include the AI detection
where_we_win.detail: In the ACT's October 2026 programme, Orikan supplies the parking solution and infringement management system (about A$64.3M) while Acusensus supplies the AI enforcement cameras on an initial five-year term of about A$63M, rising to about A$210M if both extension options are exercised. Be precise: the Acusensus scope is road-safety offences - speeding, red light, mobile phone, seatbelt, unregistered vehicles - not parking detection. The point is not that the ACT split parking detection, it is that the Territory bought specialist AI detection separately, and Orikan was not the detection vendor.

where_we_win.headline: The integration model is proven, not theoretical
where_we_win.detail: SenForce already powers gtechna's Ticket-by-Mail: SenSen cameras capture the violation, an automated workflow builds the ticket and evidence package, and the notice is mailed after officer approval. It runs live in Pittsburgh, Kitchener and Medford. A council keeping its existing infringement system is not a special case for us; it is how most of our North American base is deployed.

where_we_win.headline: Calgary retendered globally and chose us again, for up to nine years
where_we_win.detail: A customer since 2016, Calgary ran a full RFP in 2024 to replace its vehicle monitoring and enforcement technology and reselected SenSen: A$4.6M over five years with two further two-year options. That is an incumbent surviving open competition on a replacement decision, which is the exact decision this prospect is making.

where_we_win.headline: No hardware estate to buy or replace
where_we_win.detail: SenDISA runs on the cameras and VMS a city already owns. Orikan's model carries a physical fleet: Brimbank's three-year renewal covered 725 in-ground parking sensors alongside the software, and that estate has to be replaced on a cycle.

where_we_win.headline: One patrol pass, four departments
where_we_win.detail: The same drive that enforces parking also returns 40-plus road defect types with severity ratings, a versioned asset and signage catalogue, and worksite safety detection. Orikan's published suite covers parking, payments, permits, LPR and compliance, but not multi-domain city intelligence from one pass.

where_we_win.headline: Second ownership change in four years, mid-integration
where_we_win.detail: Five V Capital bought in October 2022, Orikan absorbed Global Parking Solutions USA in 2025 and UbiPark in December 2025, and EQT agreed to buy the company in July 2026 with close expected by year end. That is three integrations and two owners while customers sign multi-year renewals.

where_we_win.headline: Sovereign hosting, stated and certified
where_we_win.detail: Australian deployments run entirely from Sydney and Melbourne Azure regions, geo-redundant and IRAP Protected, with no data crossing the border at any stage. No equivalent published position from Orikan.

where_we_lose.headline: They are the statutory system of record in Victoria
where_we_lose.detail: PinForce has 200-plus ANZ local government customers and is used by 39 of Victoria's 79 councils, 35 of which have already moved to SaaS. Brimbank's officers wrote that failing to upgrade would severely impact staff ability to issue infringements in line with statutory requirements.
where_we_lose.counter: Lead with integration, not replacement. We are the detection layer that feeds their existing infringement workflow, exactly as we feed gtechna in North America. Nobody has to rip out PinForce to buy us.

where_we_lose.headline: A$64.3M of fresh territory-scale credibility
where_we_lose.detail: The ACT awarded Orikan the new parking and infringement management system on 23 October 2026, about A$64.3M on contracts running up to 15 years.
where_we_lose.counter: Read the award precisely with the prospect: Orikan won the parking and infringement system, Acusensus won the road-safety detection cameras. It is a genuine Orikan win on back office and a demonstration that the Territory buys AI detection from specialists.

where_we_lose.headline: One contract for the whole parking lifecycle
where_we_lose.detail: Meters, EziCom management, Sentinel sensors, PayStay payments, ePermits, UbiPark off-street and PinForce infringements can all be bought from one vendor, which is a real advantage in council procurement.
where_we_lose.counter: Ask what single-vendor convenience costs in detection quality, and whether the council wants its AI roadmap owned by a meter company whose new PE owner has only just promised to invest in AI.

where_we_lose.headline: Predictable, publicly benchmarked mid-market pricing
where_we_lose.detail: Councils can see what peers paid: A$206,590 ex GST over three years at Town of Victoria Park, A$284,894 at Manningham, A$337,500 inc GST at Inner West. That transparency reduces buying risk.
where_we_lose.counter: Use the same registers. Brimbank paid A$672,662 inc GST over three years just to move PinForce to SaaS and keep 725 sensors running. Frame our price against the whole estate cost, not the software line.

where_we_lose.headline: EQT capital behind product and AI
where_we_lose.detail: EQT has said it will invest in service delivery, product development, customer operations and data and AI capabilities, with the resources of a firm managing EUR 269 billion.
where_we_lose.counter: Capital buys a roadmap promise; it does not buy 21 years of deployed data fusion. Ask for their AI detection reference sites today, not the post-close plan.

where_we_lose.headline: They own the driver relationship; we are invisible to residents
where_we_lose.detail: PayStay, Orikan's driver-facing parking payment app, holds 4.7 out of 5 from 62,000 ratings on the Australian App Store. It rates the payment app rather than the enforcement platform, but where a council weighs resident-facing experience Orikan can point at 62,000 public ratings and we have no consumer product at all.
where_we_lose.counter: Concede it and separate the two decisions: the driver payment app and the detection layer are different purchases. Ask what the council wants the enforcement patrol itself to deliver, where the public app has no bearing.

landmines.question: In the ACT programme you supplied the parking and infringement system. Who supplied the AI detection cameras, and why was that bought separately?
landmines.why: The answer is Acusensus, for road-safety offences. It opens an honest conversation about whether detection and back office are the same buying decision, without overstating what the ACT actually split.

landmines.question: Your contract will transfer with the EQT acquisition. What has been committed in writing on roadmap continuity, support staffing and price escalation after close?
landmines.why: Orikan agreed to be acquired by BPEA EQT in July 2026 with close expected by the end of 2026, its second owner since October 2022.

landmines.question: Orikan has absorbed Global Parking Solutions USA and UbiPark in eighteen months. Which platform is strategic long term - Metro and EziCom, PinForce, or UbiPark?
landmines.why: Three overlapping product lines acquired in quick succession usually means one gets deprecated. The customer should know which before signing a nine-year term.

landmines.question: Your Sentinel sensors report occupancy. What detects a loading-zone breach, an accessible-bay misuse, or a faded sign that needs replacing?
landmines.why: Orikan's published sensor capability is occupancy data for wayfinding, analysis and management - not violation classification or asset condition.

landmines.question: Brimbank's renewal covered 725 in-ground sensors with the software. What is your sensor replacement cost at end of life, and who carries it?
landmines.why: Physical sensor estates carry a recurring capital liability that a camera-based detection layer does not.

objections.objection: Orikan gives us meters, payments, permits and infringements on one contract. Why add a second vendor?
objections.response: Keep Orikan for all of that. We are the detection layer that feeds it. That is how we already work in North America, where gtechna issues the ticket and SenSen supplies the AI evidence. In October the ACT bought its AI detection from a specialist too, separately from Orikan's parking and infringement system.

objections.objection: Orikan just won the ACT. They are the safe choice.
objections.response: They won the parking and infringement management system there, and it is a real win. The AI detection cameras in the same programme went to Acusensus, for road safety offences. So the Territory bought back office from Orikan and specialist AI detection from someone else.

objections.objection: PinForce is already embedded in our statutory workflow. Switching is too risky.
objections.response: Then do not switch it. We integrate through open REST APIs and webhooks into existing ticketing, permit, GIS and ERP systems, with 200-plus technology partners. The detection layer changes; your infringement system of record does not.

objections.objection: You are a micro-cap. Orikan has EQT behind it.
objections.response: Fair concern - we are around A$25M in market capitalisation. So take the operating numbers: FY26 ARR A$11.7M up 17%, record cash receipts A$16.0M, EBITDA A$2.0M up 23.6%, customer churn 5.6%, and Calgary renewing for up to nine years after a global retender. We are funded by customers rather than by a fund that needs an exit.

pricing_comparison.text: Orikan is the only vendor here whose pricing is systematically public, because Australian councils publish contract registers. Mid-size council infringement systems run A$206,590 ex GST over three years (Town of Victoria Park, up to A$621,847 over nine), A$284,894 over three years (Manningham), and A$337,500 inc GST over 3+2+2 (Inner West). Brimbank paid A$672,662 inc GST over three years for a PinForce SaaS upgrade plus 725 sensors. The ACT award is A$64.3M over up to 15 years. SenSen's disclosed city contracts sit an order of magnitude higher per deal - Calgary at A$1.9M in year one - because they are whole-of-city detection programmes rather than per-council software licences.

proof_quotes.quote: Acusensus will supply transportable and fixed enforcement cameras in the ACT while Orikan will deliver a new parking system and infringement management system.
In Victoria PinForce is used by 39 of the 79 Councils.
The inability to implement the SaaS application will severely impact the ability of staff to issue infringements in the field in line with our City Compliance statutory requirements.
The transaction is expected to close by the end of 2026 and is subject to customary regularly approvals.

battlecards.overview: Perth-based ANPR specialist taking small and mid-sized councils across Australia and New Zealand through cheap trials that convert to extensions, with ISO 27001 as its procurement calling card.
battlecards.tldr: We win when the buyer needs enforcement-grade evidence at city scale, data sovereignty, or more than parking from the patrol. We lose a single-purpose time-limited-parking job at a small council on price and speed, where a NZ$25,000 six-month trial beats a procurement process.
battlecards.quick_dismiss: Aero Ranger is genuinely good at one job: digitally chalking time-limited parking for a council with a couple of enforcement vehicles, and they are winning that job across both countries. They are a point tool - no road-condition, asset or safety capability from the same patrol. Ask what the council wants that patrol to return in three years.

where_we_win.headline: Ask for overturn rates, not accuracy claims
where_we_win.detail: Accuracy is stated by councils at about 95% for Aero Ranger; our own published figures are over 98% ALPR and 99% evidence packages, but those are self-reported and the two are not measured the same way. Ask both vendors for contested-ticket overturn rates on comparable deployments and compare like for like.

where_we_win.headline: Privacy and retention governance
where_we_win.detail: Councils publish their privacy assessments, and rigour varies by vendor. In-country hosting and clear retention rules can be a selling point.

where_we_win.headline: Sovereign hosting, certified to government standard
where_we_win.detail: Australian deployments run 100% from Sydney and Melbourne Azure regions, geo-redundant and IRAP Protected, with no data leaving Australian borders at any stage. Aero Ranger publishes ISO 27001 but no in-country hosting commitment.

where_we_win.headline: One patrol, several departments
where_we_win.detail: The same pass returns 40-plus road defect types with severity, a versioned asset and signage register, and worksite safety detection. Aero Ranger's published scope is parking, permits, inspections and evidence - a second system would be needed for the rest.

where_we_win.headline: Scale and renewal proof at city level
where_we_win.detail: Calgary ran a global retender in 2024 and reselected SenSen for up to nine years; Montreal, Toronto, Brisbane, Singapore and Philadelphia are live; FY26 brought multi-year renewals at Las Vegas, Cairns, Ipswich and Newcastle. Aero Ranger's public footprint is small and mid-sized councils, with no large-city deployment found.

where_we_lose.headline: Price and time-to-start are not close
where_we_lose.detail: Hutt City ran a two-week test and then a six-month trial for NZ$25,000 on one of four enforcement vehicles. That is a budget line a manager can approve without a tender.
where_we_lose.counter: Do not fight on trial price. Compete on the second purchase: ask what the three-year price is once the trial rate ends, and what the council does when it needs asset or road data too.

where_we_lose.headline: An established ANZ council footprint, not a recent arrival
where_we_lose.detail: Maitland City Council (NSW) has used ranger-vehicle cameras since 2023, and the footprint now spans City of Mitcham (SA), Central Coast and Glenorchy (TAS) and the Wellington-region New Zealand councils. Hutt City moved from trial to live LPR monitoring in February 2025. Treat them as an incumbent in small-council parking, not a startup.
where_we_lose.counter: Compete on what the patrol returns beyond overstay, on evidence standard when a ticket is contested, and on in-country hosting - not on footprint or tenure.

where_we_lose.headline: Trials convert, and they know it
where_we_lose.detail: Glenorchy extended for a further 12 months after a successful six-month trial, with the mayor citing greater coverage, better accuracy and reduced strain injuries from removing manual chalking.
where_we_lose.counter: Match the entry motion where it matters. Our own FY26 Darebin and Port Phillip trials are the same wedge, and we can offer a data-only first phase as Waipa bought.

where_we_lose.headline: ISO 27001 certification in hand
where_we_lose.detail: Councils explicitly cite the certification, independent surveillance audits and a formal ISMS as a reason to trust the system with personal data.
where_we_lose.counter: Concede the certification, then raise the bar: ISO 27001 certifies process, IRAP Protected plus in-country Azure certifies where Australian government data physically lives.

where_we_lose.headline: Local reach through a reseller
where_we_lose.detail: New Zealand councils are reached partly through AD Riley rather than direct, which gives a local face in procurement conversations.
where_we_lose.counter: A reseller is also a layer between the council and the people who build the product. Ask who answers when the evidence is challenged in court.

landmines.question: Will the privacy impact assessment be finalised and signed before any camera goes live, and who signs it?
landmines.why: A neutral governance question every council should put to every LPR vendor, including us. It surfaces process rigour early.

landmines.question: What image retention period is proposed, and how does it compare with the legal minimum for parking infringement evidence?
landmines.why: Retention proposals vary against the one-year legal minimum for infringement evidence, and the council carries the privacy exposure, not the vendor.

landmines.question: What documented process stops reviewers from rubber-stamping the AI?
landmines.why: Automation bias is the standard risk in human-in-the-loop enforcement: a reviewer assuming the tool is right because it usually is. Ask for the documented control.

landmines.question: What is your contested-ticket overturn rate on a comparable deployment, and how is accuracy measured?
landmines.why: Turns differing accuracy claims into one comparable operational number.

landmines.question: When the council wants road-condition, signage and asset data from the same patrol, is that a second contract?
landmines.why: Aero Ranger's published scope is parking and local-laws compliance; ours returns asset and road data from the same drive.

objections.objection: Aero Ranger is a fraction of your price.
objections.response: For one job at one council, yes. The comparison changes when the same patrol has to produce road-condition, signage and asset data, because that becomes a second system and a second contract. Price the programme, not the camera.

objections.objection: Councils around us already use them.
objections.response: They do, and they have for years - Maitland has run ranger-vehicle cameras since 2023, alongside Mitcham, Central Coast, Glenorchy and the Wellington-region councils. They are a credible choice for time-limited parking. The question is what the council wants from the patrol beyond overstay detection, and who carries the evidence standard when a ticket is challenged.

objections.objection: They are ISO 27001 certified. Are you?
objections.response: ISO 27001 certifies that a security process exists. For Australian government data the question is where it lives: our Australian deployments run 100% from Sydney and Melbourne Azure regions, geo-redundant, IRAP Protected, with nothing crossing the border at any stage.

objections.objection: Their system already does human review, same as yours.
objections.response: Same principle. Ask both vendors for contested-ticket overturn rates on comparable deployments.

objections.objection: Our neighbours trialled them and it worked fine. Why change?
objections.response: Trials prove overstay detection, which they do well. Ask what happens at renewal when the council wants road-condition and asset data from the same patrol, and what the evidence standard is when a ticket is contested.

pricing_comparison.text: Aero Ranger lands through low-cost trials: NZ$25,000 bought Hutt City a six-month trial on one of four enforcement vehicles, after a free two-week test. Glenorchy's 12-month extension and Waipa's three-month data-only trial were not priced publicly. Our disclosed contracts are whole-of-city programmes an order of magnitude larger - Calgary at A$1.9M in year one and A$4.6M over five years - so the two rarely meet in the same tender unless a small council is deciding between a point tool and a platform.

proof_quotes.quote: It is around 95% accurate, and every potential breach is checked by a real person before any ticket is issued.
Aero Ranger allows our officers to cover more ground with greater accuracy, which means better compliance and a fairer outcome for everyone using our parking spaces.
new cutting edge licence plate recognition technology known as AeroRanger, which will see two cameras mounted on to ranger vehicles

white_space.opportunity: Sell the AI detection layer separately from the infringement back office
white_space.evidence: SenSen already runs this model in North America, where gtechna issues the ticket and SenSen supplies the AI evidence. The ACT's October 2026 programme shows a major government buyer doing the same structurally: specialist AI detection (Acusensus, road safety) bought separately from the parking and infringement system (Orikan).

white_space.opportunity: Multi-department value from one patrol pass, priced as a city programme rather than a parking licence
white_space.evidence: No competitor publishes road-condition, asset-register and worksite-safety detection from the same drive. Orikan's suite stops at parking and compliance; Aero Ranger's at parking, permits and inspections.

white_space.opportunity: Privacy and retention governance as a selling feature in ANZ council procurement
white_space.evidence: ANZ councils publish their privacy impact assessments, and rigour varies by vendor and deployment. A vendor that leads with in-country hosting, a stated retention policy and a documented review process removes a procurement unknown. SenSen's Australian deployments run entirely from Sydney and Melbourne Azure regions, IRAP Protected, with policy-driven retention.

white_space.opportunity: The Victorian metro council segment, where incumbency is strong but AI detection is absent
white_space.evidence: PinForce is the infringement system in 39 of Victoria's 79 councils, yet Orikan publishes no AI capture-to-citation capability. SenSen only began metro Melbourne trials with Darebin and Port Phillip in FY26, so the segment is still open.

Orikan's council pricing is already public through contract registers, from A$206,590 to A$672,662 over three years. A vendor that publishes indicative pricing removes a procurement unknown that currently favours the incumbent.

changes.change: Orikan won the ACT Government parking and infringement management system, about A$64.3M over contracts of up to 15 years, announced 23 October 2026. The AI enforcement cameras in the same programme went to Acusensus for road-safety offences, on an initial five-year term of about A$63M rising to about A$210M with extensions.
changes.why_it_matters: A major back-office win for Orikan, and evidence that government buyers purchase specialist AI detection separately from the parking vendor.
changes.rep_action: State the split precisely - Acusensus detection is road safety, not parking - or the point will be corrected in the room.

changes.change: EQT agreed in July 2026 to acquire Orikan from Five V Capital, with close expected by the end of 2026 - Orikan's second private-equity owner since October 2022.
changes.why_it_matters: Second PE owner since 2022 means roadmap and support commitments are unsettled during renewals.
changes.rep_action: Ask what is committed in writing on roadmap and support staffing after close.

changes.change: Orikan acquired UbiPark in December 2025 and completed the Global Parking Solutions USA acquisition in 2025, adding two product lines to integrate alongside PinForce.
changes.why_it_matters: Three overlapping product lines in eighteen months usually means one gets deprecated.
changes.rep_action: Ask which platform is strategic long term before they sign a multi-year term.

changes.change: SenSen FY26: ARR A$11.7M up 17%, record cash receipts A$16.0M, EBITDA A$2.0M up 23.6%, but revenue only slightly ahead of the prior year as NVIDIA hardware supply issues pushed Singapore and Australian projects into FY27.
changes.why_it_matters: Flat revenue and delayed projects weaken the growth story a prospect may check.
changes.rep_action: Lead with ARR, EBITDA and churn, not headline revenue; name the supply-chain cause if asked.

changes.change: SenSen disclosed FY26 customer churn of 5.6%, against a long-running investor narrative of negligible churn.
changes.why_it_matters: Contradicts the negligible-churn narrative, so never claim zero churn in a deal.
changes.rep_action: Say 5.6% and that it is low for government software; do not overclaim.

changes.change: SenSen opened its first metropolitan Melbourne council trials with Darebin and Port Phillip, moving directly into Orikan's strongest segment.
changes.why_it_matters: Puts us directly into Orikan's strongest segment, where PinForce is the system of record.
changes.rep_action: Position as integrating with PinForce, not replacing it.

changes.change: Aero Ranger expanded through six New Zealand councils in under two years and sponsored the South Australian LGAPA conference in August 2026, signalling a South Australian push.
changes.why_it_matters: Peer-reference momentum in small councils compounds and will reach mid-market next.
changes.rep_action: Counter the peer-reference motion with the published Hutt City privacy assessment.

notes.Research method: Research method: Exa neural search over primary sources, then direct reading of ASX filings, council contract registers, council meeting minutes, LGOIMA releases and trade press. This replaces the keyword-and-review-site collection the automated run used, which found zero independent sources for SenSen.ai.
notes.Structural finding: Structural finding: these three vendors are not competing at the same layer. SenSen is a detection and intelligence layer, Orikan is the infringement back office plus hardware, and Aero Ranger is a single-purpose mobile enforcement tool. Most ANZ deals are therefore integration questions, not displacement questions.
notes.Where the pricing comes from: Pricing in this report comes from public Australian council contract registers and New Zealand council disclosures, not from vendor marketing. Orikan's prices are systematically visible because councils must publish them; SenSen's come from ASX disclosures; Aero Ranger's single public figure is the Hutt City trial.
notes.Open question: Orikan ownership: Unresolved: Five V Capital stated in July 2026 that the EQT transaction was expected to close by the end of 2026, while at least one wire report described it as completed. Confirm completion status before using the ownership-transition landmine in a live deal.
notes.Why the rating charts are empty: Market reputation here is employer reputation, not product reviews. None of the three vendors is listed on G2 or Capterra's parking management category, where peers are rated (gtechna 4.4 from 18 reviews, Parkable 4.9 from 98), so the absence is real rather than a collection gap. Indeed covers both SenSen.ai and Orikan and is therefore used for the scored comparison, so the head-to-head is like-for-like. Glassdoor data is cited in the profiles rather than scored, because SenSen's global Glassdoor figure could not be verified and scoring a site only one company appears on would distort the leader badge. Aero Ranger has no employer-review presence at all, consistent with 16 staff.
notes.How to read Who leads where: Capability rows are tagged to the five buying categories that have evidence here: product, pricing, support, implementation and integrations. A cell marked no evidence is excluded from scoring rather than counted as a zero, so a vendor is never penalised for not publishing something.
notes.Where the real customer verdict lives: In this market the customer verdict is revealed by procurement, not reviews, and it is already in this report: Calgary ran a global retender in 2024 and reselected SenSen for up to nine years; FY26 brought multi-year renewals at Las Vegas, Cairns, Ipswich and Newcastle against 5.6% churn; Glenorchy extended Aero Ranger for 12 months after a six-month trial; and 35 of 39 Victorian PinForce councils chose to carry Orikan forward to SaaS. Read those as the satisfaction signal. They are stronger evidence than a star rating because a council backs them with budget.
notes.Buyer reviews: No meaningful buyer reviews exist in this category. None of the three vendors is listed on G2 or Capterra's parking management category, where peers are rated (gtechna 4.4 from 18 reviews, Parkable 4.9 from 98). Employer-review sites and Orikan's PayStay consumer app both carry ratings, but neither tells you how a council buyer rates the product, so neither is scored here. Rating and Market voice are deliberately left unscored.
notes.The ACT contract, stated precisely: The ACT announced the contracts on 23 October 2026; press coverage followed on 26-27 October. Orikan won the parking solution and infringement management system at about A$64.3M over contracts running up to 15 years. Acusensus won the enforcement cameras on an initial five-year term of about A$63M, rising to about A$210M if both extension options are exercised, per its ASX announcement; one press account instead reported the Acusensus value as about A$191M, and this report uses the ASX figure throughout. The Acusensus scope is road-safety offences - speeding, red light, mobile phone, seatbelt, unregistered vehicles - not parking detection. It is therefore wrong to say the ACT split parking detection from the back office. What it shows is a government buyer purchasing specialist AI detection separately from its parking and infringement vendor. Staged rollout starts mid-2027.
notes.Accuracy figures are not like-for-like: SenSen's 98-99% accuracy figures are self-published. Aero Ranger's ~95% is stated by councils. Orikan publishes no accuracy figure. These are not comparable, so the card asks every vendor for a contested-ticket overturn rate on a comparable deployment instead of ranking them.
